More serious symptoms include intermittent claudication, angina pectoris, and transient ischaemic attacks.1 Patients often present with either arterial or venous thrombosis (cerebrovascular accident, myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism) or occasionally, with haemorrhage, particularly involv- ing the skin and gastrointestinal tract; splenic pain or gout may also be presenting features.1,4 Untreated, the disease is associated with a high risk of morbidity and mortality, and patients can undergo mye- lofibrotic transformation into blast crisis and acute mye- loid leukaemia.1,4 The aims of treatment are therefore to reduce the risk of thrombosis and haemorrhage, minimise transformation risk, and manage complications, or preg- nancy.4 The mainstay of treatment is periodic phlebotomy to main- tain the haematocrit within normal values,5,6 along with aspirin in low doses (40 to 100 mg daily)1 sufficient to re- duce thrombosis without increasing the risk of major bleeding.7 This may be all that is required in younger pa- tients at low risk of thrombosis. In patients at high risk of thrombosis, including those who have a high phlebotomy requirement, some form of myelosuppressive therapy may also be considered. Chlorambucil, which was formerly used for this purpose, has largely been stopped because of a high incidence of leukaemia in patients so treated.4-6 In patients with a life expectancy of less than 10 years, radio- active phosphorus-32 is probably appropriate, and produc- es good results with few immediate adverse effects.5,8 However, like the alkylating agents it is associated with an increased risk of secondary malignancies.6 In younger pa- tients hydroxycarbamide,1,4,6,8 busulfan,5,6 or in some countries pipobroman,5,9 have been preferred because they were considered to have lower risk of inducing leukaemia. However, there is some evidence9,10 that they too may have leukaemogenic potential, especially when used in combination,11 and some recommend that busulfan and pipobroman be reserved for elderly patients.1,4 Non-cyto- toxic therapies that have been shown to be effective in- clude interferon alfa.1,4-6,10,12 This may be preferred in younger patients requiring treatment.4,5,8 Anagrelide, an- other antiplatelet drug, has also been tried in polycythae- mia vera. It is effective in controlling the platelet count, but does not control progression of polycythaemia vera, and its adverse effects may make it difficult for some patients to tolerate.4 1.
